{{short description|Technique to make a model more generalizable and transferable}}
[[File:Regularization.svg|thumb|250px|The green and blue functions both incur zero loss on the given data points. A learned model can be induced to prefer the green function, which may generalize better to more points drawn from the underlying unknown distribution, by adjusting <math>\lambda</math>, the weight of the regularization term.]]
In [[mathematics]], [[statistics]], [[Mathematical finance|finance]],<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.3390/risks8020040 |title=Deep Arbitrage-Free Learning in a Generalized HJM Framework via Arbitrage-Regularization Data|journal=Risks |year=2020 |last1=Kratsios |first1=Anastasis  |volume=8|issue=2|page=[https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9091/8/2/40] |quote=Term structure models can be regularized to remove arbitrage {{sic|?|opportunities}}.|doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.11850/456375 |hdl-access=free |arxiv=1710.05114 }}</ref> and [[computer science]], particularly in [[machine learning]] and [[inverse problem]]s, '''regularization''' is a process that converts the [[Problem solving|answer to a problem]] to a simpler one. It is often used in solving [[ill-posed problems]] or to prevent [[overfitting]].<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-20192-9 |title=Statistics for High-Dimensional Data|url=https://archive.org/details/statisticsforhig00bhlm |url-access=limited |series=Springer Series in Statistics |year=2011 |last1=Bühlmann |first1=Peter |last2=Van De Geer |first2=Sara |isbn=978-3-642-20191-2 |page=[https://archive.org/details/statisticsforhig00bhlm/page/n27 9] |quote=If p > n, the ordinary least squares estimator is not unique and will heavily overfit the data. Thus, a form of complexity regularization will be necessary.}}</ref> There is a strong connection between regularization methods and Bayesian approaches for solving such ill-posed problems.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Huang | first1 = Yunfei. | display-authors = etal | year = 2019 | title = Traction force microscopy with optimized regularization and automated Bayesian parameter selection for comparing cells | journal = Scientific Reports | volume = 9 | number = 1| page = 537 | article-number = 539 | doi = 10.1038/s41598-018-36896-x | pmid = 30679578 | doi-access = free | pmc = 6345967 | arxiv = 1810.05848 | bibcode = 2019NatSR...9..539H }}</ref>

Although regularization procedures can be divided in many ways, the following delineation is particularly helpful:
* '''Explicit regularization''' is regularization whenever one explicitly adds a term to the optimization problem.  These terms could be [[Prior probability|priors]], penalties, or constraints. Explicit regularization is commonly employed with ill-posed optimization problems. The regularization term, or penalty, imposes a cost on the optimization function to make the optimal solution unique.
* '''Implicit regularization''' is all other forms of regularization.  This includes, for example, early stopping, using a robust loss function, and discarding outliers. Implicit regularization is essentially ubiquitous in modern machine learning approaches, including [[stochastic gradient descent]] for training [[deep neural networks]], and [[ensemble methods]] (such as [[random forest]]s and [[gradient boosted trees]]).

In explicit regularization, independent of the problem or model, there is always a data term, that corresponds to a likelihood of the measurement, and a regularization term that corresponds to a prior. By combining both using [[Bayesian statistics]], one can compute a posterior, that includes both information sources and therefore stabilizes the estimation process. By trading off both objectives, one chooses to be more aligned to the data or to enforce regularization (to prevent overfitting). There is a whole research branch dealing with all possible regularizations. In practice, one usually tries a specific regularization and then figures out the probability density that corresponds to that regularization to justify the choice. It can also be physically motivated by common sense or intuition.

In [[supervised learning|machine learning]], the data term corresponds to the training data and the regularization is either the choice of the model or modifications to the algorithm. It is always intended to reduce the [[generalization error]], i.e. the error score with the trained model on the evaluation set (testing data) and not the training data.<ref>{{Cite book| first1 = Ian | last1 = Goodfellow | first2 = Yoshua | last2 = Bengio | first3 = Aaron | last3 = Courville | date= | title = Deep Learning Book | url = https://www.deeplearningbook.org/contents/ml.html | access-date = 2021-01-29}}</ref>

One of the earliest uses of regularization is [[Tikhonov regularization]] (ridge regression), related to the method of least squares.

== Regularization in machine learning ==
In [[machine learning]], a key challenge is enabling models to accurately predict outcomes on unseen data, not just on familiar training data. Regularization is crucial for addressing [[overfitting]]—where a model memorizes training data details but cannot generalize to new data. The goal of regularization is to encourage models to learn the broader patterns within the data rather than memorizing it. Techniques like [[early stopping]], L1 and [[L2 regularization]], and [[Dropout (neural networks)|dropout]] are designed to prevent overfitting and underfitting, thereby enhancing the model's ability to adapt to and perform well with new data, thus improving model generalization.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Guo |first=Jingru |title=AI Notes: Regularizing neural networks |url=https://deeplearning.ai/ai-notes/regularization/ |access-date=2024-02-04 |website=[[deeplearning.ai]]}}</ref>

=== Early stopping ===
Stops training when validation performance deteriorates, preventing overfitting by halting before the model memorizes training data.<ref name=":1" />

=== L1 and L2 regularization ===
Adds penalty terms to the cost function to discourage complex models:

* '''L1 regularization''' (also called [[Lasso (statistics)|LASSO]]) leads to [[Sparse matrix|sparse models]] by adding a penalty based on the absolute value of coefficients.
* '''L2 regularization''' (also called [[ridge regression]]) encourages smaller, more evenly distributed weights by adding a penalty based on the square of the coefficients.<ref name=":1" />

=== Dropout ===
In the context of neural networks, the Dropout technique repeatedly ignores random subsets of neurons during training, which simulates the training of multiple neural network architectures at once to improve generalization.<ref name=":1" />

== Classification ==

Empirical learning of classifiers (from a finite data set) is always an [[Underdetermination|underdetermined]] problem, because it attempts to infer a function of any <math>x</math> given only examples <math>x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n</math>.

A regularization term (or regularizer) <math>R(f)</math> is added to a [[Loss functions for classification|loss function]]:
<math display="block">\min_f \sum_{i=1}^{n} V(f(x_i), y_i) + \lambda R(f)</math>
where <math>V</math> is an underlying loss function that describes the cost of predicting <math>f(x)</math> when the label is <math>y</math>, such as the [[Loss functions for classification#Square loss|square loss]] or [[hinge loss]]; and <math>\lambda</math> is a parameter which controls the importance of the regularization term. <math>R(f)</math> is typically chosen to impose a penalty on the complexity of <math>f</math>. Concrete notions of complexity used include restrictions for [[smooth function|smoothness]] and bounds on the [[normed vector space|vector space norm]].<ref name=":0" />{{page needed|date=May 2017}}

A theoretical justification for regularization is that it attempts to impose [[Occam's razor]] on the solution (as depicted in the figure above, where the green function, the simpler one, may be preferred). From a [[Bayesian inference|Bayesian]] point of view, many regularization techniques correspond to imposing certain [[prior probability|prior]] distributions on model parameters.<ref>For the connection between [[maximum a posteriori estimation]] and [[ridge regression]], see {{cite web |first=Kilian |last=Weinberger |title=Linear / Ridge Regression |publisher=Cornell |work=CS4780 Machine Learning Lecture 13 |date=July 11, 2018 |url=https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs4780/2018fa/lectures/lecturenote08.html#map-estimate }}</ref>

Regularization can serve multiple purposes, including learning simpler models, inducing models to be sparse and introducing group structure{{clarify|reason=What is structure in the learning process?|date=October 2018}} into the learning problem.

The same idea arose in many fields of [[science]]. A simple form of regularization applied to [[integral equation]]s ([[Tikhonov regularization]])  is essentially a trade-off between fitting the data and reducing a norm of the solution. More recently, non-linear regularization methods, including [[total variation regularization]], have become popular.

=== Generalization ===
{{Main|Generalization error}}

Regularization can be motivated as a technique to improve the generalizability of a learned model.

The goal of this learning problem is to find a function that fits or predicts the outcome (label) that minimizes the expected error over all possible inputs and labels. The expected error of a function <math>f_n</math> is:
<math display="block"> I[f_n] = \int_{X \times Y} V(f_n(x),y) \rho(x,y) \, dx \, dy </math>
where <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are the domains of input data <math>x</math> and their labels <math>y</math> respectively.

Typically in learning problems, only a subset of input data and labels are available, measured with some noise. Therefore, the expected error is unmeasurable, and the best surrogate available is the empirical error over the <math> N </math> available samples:
<math display="block"> I_S[f_n] = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^N V(f_n(\hat x_i), \hat y_i) </math>
Without bounds on the complexity of the function space (formally, the [[reproducing kernel Hilbert space]]) available, a model will be learned that incurs zero loss on the surrogate empirical error. If measurements (e.g. of <math>x_i</math>) were made with noise, this model may suffer from [[overfitting]] and display poor expected error. Regularization introduces a penalty for exploring certain regions of the function space used to build the model, which can improve generalization.

== Tikhonov regularization (ridge regression) ==
{{Main|Tikhonov regularization}}
These techniques are named for [[Andrey Nikolayevich Tikhonov]], who applied regularization to [[integral equation]]s and made important contributions in many other areas.

When learning a linear function <math>f</math>, characterized by an unknown [[Vector space|vector]] <math>w</math> such that <math>f(x) = w \cdot x</math>, one can add the <math>L_2</math>-norm of the vector <math>w</math> to the loss expression in order to prefer solutions with smaller norms. Tikhonov regularization is one of the most common forms. It is also known as ridge regression. It is expressed as:
<math display="block">\min_w \sum_{i=1}^{n} V(\hat x_i \cdot w, \hat y_i) + \lambda \left\|w\right\|_2^2,</math>
where <math>(\hat x_i, \hat y_i), \, 1 \leq i \leq n,</math> would represent samples used for training.

In the case of a general function, the norm of the function in its [[reproducing kernel Hilbert space]] is:
<math display="block">\min_f \sum_{i=1}^{n} V(f(\hat x_i), \hat y_i) + \lambda \left\|f\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2</math>

As the <math>L_2</math> norm is [[Differentiable function#Differentiability in higher dimensions|differentiable]], learning can be advanced by [[gradient descent]].

=== Tikhonov-regularized least squares ===
The learning problem with the [[least squares]] loss function and Tikhonov regularization can be solved analytically. Written in matrix form, the optimal <math>w</math> is the one for which the gradient of the loss function with respect to <math>w</math> is 0.
<math display="block">\min_w \frac{1}{n} \left(\hat X w - Y\right)^\mathsf{T} \left(\hat X w - Y\right) + \lambda \left\|w\right\|_2^2</math>
<math display="block">\nabla_w = \frac{2}{n} \hat X^\mathsf{T} \left(\hat X w -  Y\right) + 2 \lambda w</math>
<math display="block">0 = \hat X^\mathsf{T} \left(\hat X w -  Y\right) + n \lambda w</math><math display="block">w = \left(\hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat X + \lambda n I\right)^{-1} \left(\hat X^\mathsf{T} Y\right)</math>
where the third statement is a [[first-order condition]].

By construction of the optimization problem, other values of <math>w</math> give larger values for the loss function. This can be verified by examining the [[second derivative]] <math>\nabla_{ww}</math>.

During training, this algorithm takes <math>O(d^3 + n d^2)</math> [[Time complexity|time]]. The terms correspond to the matrix inversion and calculating <math>X^\mathsf{T} X</math>, respectively. Testing takes <math>O(nd)</math> time.

== Early stopping ==
{{Main|Early stopping}}
Early stopping can be viewed as regularization in time. Intuitively, a training procedure such as gradient descent tends to learn more and more complex functions with increasing iterations. By regularizing for time, model complexity can be controlled, improving generalization.

Early stopping is implemented using one data set for training, one statistically independent data set for validation and another for testing. The model is trained until performance on the validation set no longer improves and then applied to the test set.

=== Theoretical motivation in least squares ===
Consider the finite approximation of [[Neumann series]] for an invertible matrix {{mvar|A}} where <math>\left\| I - A \right\| < 1</math>:
<math display="block">\sum_{i=0}^{T-1} \left(I - A\right)^i \approx A^{-1}</math>

This can be used to approximate the analytical solution of unregularized least squares, if {{mvar|γ}} is introduced to ensure the norm is less than one.
<math display="block">w_T = \frac{\gamma}{n} \sum_{i=0}^{T-1} \left( I - \frac{\gamma}{n} \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat X \right)^i \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat Y</math>

The exact solution to the unregularized least squares learning problem minimizes the empirical error, but may fail. By limiting {{mvar|T}}, the only free parameter in the algorithm above, the problem is regularized for time, which may improve its generalization.

The algorithm above is equivalent to restricting the number of gradient descent iterations for the empirical risk
<math display="block">I_s[w] = \frac{1}{2n} \left\| \hat X w - \hat Y \right\|^{2}_{\mathbb{R}^n}</math>
with the gradient descent update:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
w_0 &= 0 \\[1ex]
w_{t+1} &= \left(I - \frac{\gamma}{n} \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat X\right) w_t + \frac{\gamma}{n} \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat Y
\end{align}</math>

The base case is trivial. The inductive case is proved as follows:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
w_{T} &= \left(I - \frac{\gamma}{n} \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat X\right) \frac{\gamma}{n} \sum_{i=0}^{T-2} \left(I - \frac{\gamma}{n} \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat X \right)^i \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat Y + \frac{\gamma}{n}\hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat Y
\\[1ex]
&= \frac{\gamma}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{T-1} \left(I - \frac{\gamma}{n} \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat X \right)^i \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat Y + \frac{\gamma}{n}\hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat Y
\\[1ex]
&= \frac{\gamma}{n} \sum_{i=0}^{T-1} \left(I - \frac{\gamma}{n} \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat X \right)^i \hat X^\mathsf{T} \hat Y
\end{align}</math>

== Regularizers for sparsity ==
Assume that a dictionary <math>\phi_j</math> with dimension <math>p</math> is given such that a function in the function space can be expressed as:
<math display="block">f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{p} \phi_j(x) w_j</math>

[[File:Sparsityl1.png|thumb|A comparison between the L1 ball and the L2 ball in two dimensions gives an intuition on how L1 regularization achieves sparsity.]]

Enforcing a sparsity constraint on <math>w</math> can lead to simpler and more interpretable models. This is useful in many real-life applications such as [[computational biology]]. An example is developing a simple predictive test for a disease in order to minimize the cost of performing medical tests while maximizing predictive power.

A sensible sparsity constraint is the [[Norm (mathematics)|<math>L_0</math> norm]] <math>\|w\|_0</math>, defined as the number of non-zero elements in <math>w</math>. Solving a <math>L_0</math> regularized learning problem, however, has been demonstrated to be [[NP-hardness|NP-hard]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Natarajan|first=B.|date=1995-04-01|title=Sparse Approximate Solutions to Linear Systems|url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/S0097539792240406|journal=SIAM Journal on Computing |volume=24|issue=2|pages=227–234|doi=10.1137/S0097539792240406|s2cid=2072045 |issn=0097-5397|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The [[Taxicab geometry|<math>L_1</math> norm]] (see also [[Norm (mathematics)|Norms]]) can be used to approximate the optimal [[Norm (mathematics)|<math>L_0</math>]] norm via convex relaxation. It can be shown that the [[Norm (mathematics)|<math>L_1</math>]] norm induces sparsity. In the case of least squares, this problem is known as [[Lasso (statistics)|LASSO]] in statistics and [[basis pursuit]] in signal processing.
<math display="block">\min_{w \in \mathbb{R}^p} \frac{1}{n} \left\|\hat X w - \hat Y \right\|^2 + \lambda \left\|w\right\|_{1}</math>

[[File:Sparsityen.png|thumb|Elastic net regularization]]

[[Norm (mathematics)|<math>L_1</math>]] regularization can occasionally produce non-unique solutions. A simple example is provided in the figure when the space of possible solutions lies on a 45 degree line. This can be problematic for certain applications, and is overcome by combining [[Norm (mathematics)|<math>L_1</math>]] with [[Norm (mathematics)|<math>L_2</math>]] regularization in [[elastic net regularization]], which takes the following form:
<math display="block">\min_{w \in \mathbb{R}^p} \frac{1}{n} \left\|\hat X w - \hat Y \right\|^2 + \lambda \left(\alpha \left\|w\right\|_1 + (1 - \alpha)\left\|w\right\|_2^2\right), \alpha \in [0, 1]</math>

Elastic net regularization tends to have a grouping effect, where correlated input features are assigned equal weights.

Elastic net regularization is commonly used in practice and is implemented in many machine learning libraries.

=== Proximal methods ===
{{Main|Proximal gradient method}}While the [[Norm (mathematics)|<math>L_1</math>]] norm does not result in an NP-hard problem, the [[Norm (mathematics)|<math>L_1</math>]] norm is convex but is not strictly differentiable due to the kink at x = 0. [[Subgradient method]]s which rely on the [[subderivative]] can be used to solve [[Norm (mathematics)|<math>L_1</math>]] regularized learning problems. However, faster convergence can be achieved through proximal methods.

For a problem <math>\min_{w \in H} F(w) + R(w)</math> such that <math>F</math> is convex, continuous, differentiable, with Lipschitz continuous gradient (such as the least squares loss function), and <math>R</math> is convex, continuous, and proper, then the proximal method to solve the problem is as follows. First define the [[proximal operator]]
<math display="block">\operatorname{prox}_R(v) = \mathop\operatorname{argmin}_{w \in \mathbb{R}^D} \left\{ R(w) + \frac{1}{2} \left\|w - v\right\|^2 \right\}, </math>
and then iterate
<math display="block">w_{k+1} = \mathop\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma, R} \left(w_k - \gamma \nabla F(w_k)\right)</math>

The proximal method iteratively performs gradient descent and then projects the result back into the space permitted by <math>R</math>.

When <math>R</math> is the [[Norm (mathematics)|{{math|''L''<sub>1</sub>}}]] regularizer, the proximal operator is equivalent to the soft-thresholding operator,
<math display="block">S_\lambda(v)f(n) = \begin{cases}
v_i - \lambda, & \text{if }v_i > \lambda \\
0, & \text{if } v_i \in [-\lambda, \lambda] \\
v_i + \lambda, & \text{if }v_i < - \lambda
\end{cases}</math>

This allows for efficient computation.

=== Group sparsity without overlaps ===
Groups of features can be regularized by a sparsity constraint, which can be useful for expressing certain prior knowledge into an optimization problem.

In the case of a linear model with non-overlapping known groups, a regularizer can be defined:
<math display="block">R(w) = \sum_{g=1}^G \left\|w_g\right\|_2,</math> where <math display="block">\|w_g\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{|G_g|} \left(w_g^j\right)^2}</math>

This can be viewed as inducing a regularizer over the <math>L_2</math> norm over members of each group followed by an <math>L_1</math> norm over groups.

This can be solved by the proximal method, where the proximal operator is a block-wise soft-thresholding function:

<math display="block">\operatorname{prox}\limits_{\lambda, R, g}(w_g) = \begin{cases}
 \left(1 - \dfrac{\lambda}{\left\|w_g\right\|_2}\right) w_g, & \text{if } \left\|w_g\right\|_2 > \lambda \\[1ex]
 0, & \text{if } \|w_g\|_2 \leq \lambda
\end{cases}</math>

=== Group sparsity with overlaps ===
The algorithm described for group sparsity without overlaps can be applied to the case where groups do overlap, in certain situations. This will likely result in some groups with all zero elements, and other groups with some non-zero and some zero elements.

If it is desired to preserve the group structure, a new regularizer can be defined:
<math display="block">R(w) = \inf \left\{ \sum_{g=1}^G \|w_g\|_2 : w = \sum_{g=1}^G \bar w_g \right\}</math>

For each <math>w_g</math>, <math>\bar w_g</math> is defined as the vector such that the restriction of <math>\bar w_g</math> to the group <math>g</math> equals <math>w_g</math> and all other entries of <math>\bar w_g</math> are zero. The regularizer finds the optimal disintegration of <math>w</math> into parts. It can be viewed as duplicating all elements that exist in multiple groups. Learning problems with this regularizer can also be solved with the proximal method with a complication. The proximal operator cannot be computed in closed form, but can be effectively solved iteratively, inducing an inner iteration within the proximal method iteration.

== Regularizers for semi-supervised learning ==
{{Main|Semi-supervised learning}}

When labels are more expensive to gather than input examples, semi-supervised learning can be useful. Regularizers have been designed to guide learning algorithms to learn models that respect the structure of unsupervised training samples. If a symmetric weight matrix <math>W</math> is given, a regularizer can be defined:
<math display="block">R(f) = \sum_{i,j} w_{ij} \left(f(x_i) - f(x_j)\right)^2</math>

If <math>W_{ij}</math> encodes the result of some distance metric for points <math>x_i</math> and <math>x_j</math>, it is desirable that <math>f(x_i) \approx f(x_j)</math>. This regularizer captures this intuition, and is equivalent to:
<math display="block">R(f) = \bar f^\mathsf{T} L \bar f</math> where <math>L = D- W</math> is the [[Laplacian matrix]] of the graph induced by <math>W</math>.

The optimization problem <math>\min_{f \in \mathbb{R}^m} R(f), m = u + l</math> can be solved analytically if the constraint <math>f(x_i) = y_i</math> is applied for all supervised samples. The labeled part of the vector <math>f</math> is therefore obvious. The unlabeled part of <math>f</math> is solved for by:
<math display="block">\min_{f_u \in \mathbb{R}^u} f^\mathsf{T} L f = \min_{f_u \in \mathbb{R}^u} \left\{ f^\mathsf{T}_u L_{uu} f_u + f^\mathsf{T}_l L_{lu} f_u + f^\mathsf{T}_u L_{ul} f_l \right\}</math>
<math display="block">\nabla_{f_u} = 2L_{uu}f_u + 2L_{ul}Y</math>
<math display="block">f_u = L_{uu}^\dagger \left(L_{ul} Y\right)</math>
The pseudo-inverse can be taken because <math>L_{ul}</math> has the same range as <math>L_{uu}</math>.

== Regularizers for multitask learning ==
{{Main|Multi-task learning}}In the case of multitask learning, <math>T</math> problems are considered simultaneously, each related in some way. The goal is to learn <math>T</math> functions, ideally borrowing strength from the relatedness of tasks, that have predictive power. This is equivalent to learning the matrix <math>W: T \times D</math> .

=== Sparse regularizer on columns ===
<math display="block">R(w) = \sum_{i=1}^D \left\|W\right\|_{2,1}</math>

This regularizer defines an L2 norm on each column and an L1 norm over all columns. It can be solved by proximal methods.

=== Nuclear norm regularization ===
<math display="block">R(w) = \left\|\sigma(W)\right\|_1</math> where <math>\sigma(W)</math> is the [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalues]] in the [[singular value decomposition]] of <math>W</math>.

=== Mean-constrained regularization ===
<math display="block">R(f_1 \cdots f_T) = \sum_{t=1}^T \left\|f_t - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{s=1}^T f_s \right\|_{H_k}^2</math>

This regularizer constrains the functions learned for each task to be similar to the overall average of the functions across all tasks. This is useful for expressing prior information that each task is expected to share with each other task. An example is predicting blood iron levels measured at different times of the day, where each task represents an individual.

=== Clustered mean-constrained regularization ===
<math display="block">R(f_1 \cdots f_T) = \sum_{r=1}^C \sum_{t \in I(r)} \left\|f_t - \frac{1}{I(r)} \sum_{s \in I(r)} f_s\right\|_{H_k}^2</math> where <math>I(r)</math> is a cluster of tasks.

This regularizer is similar to the mean-constrained regularizer, but instead enforces similarity between tasks within the same cluster. This can capture more complex prior information. This technique has been used to predict [[Netflix]] recommendations. A cluster would correspond to a group of people who share similar preferences.

=== Graph-based similarity ===
More generally than above, similarity between tasks can be defined by a function. The regularizer encourages the model to learn similar functions for similar tasks.
<math display="block">R(f_1 \cdots f_T) = \sum_{t,s=1, t \neq s}^\mathsf{T} \left\| f_t - f_s \right\|^2 M_{ts} </math> for a given symmetric [[similarity matrix]] <math>M</math>.

== Other uses of regularization in statistics and machine learning ==
[[Bayesian model comparison|Bayesian learning]] methods make use of a [[prior probability]] that (usually) gives lower probability to more complex models. Well-known model selection techniques include the [[Akaike information criterion]] (AIC), [[minimum description length]] (MDL), and the [[Bayesian information criterion]] (BIC). Alternative methods of controlling overfitting not involving regularization include [[cross-validation (statistics)|cross-validation]].
